title: Talk Moves
subtitle: A small set of teacher moves that turn “calling on kids” into a real mathematical conversation. The discourse glue inside every opener routine.

sections.label: What it is
sections.sources: Sources: Chapin, O’Connor & Anderson, Classroom Discussions in Math (2009) · NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014) · Smith & Stein, 5 Practices (2011).

blocks.text: What it is

Talk moves are **specific, repeatable things a teacher says** to get students reasoning out loud, listening to one another, and building on each other’s thinking — instead of just answering the teacher one at a time.

They are the difference between a routine that works and one that fizzles. A Number Talk, an Error Analysis, a Same But Different — *none* of them produce real discourse on their own. The talk moves are what make the conversation happen. Without them, the routine collapses back into the teacher and the same three confident hands. That is why this is a **cross-cutting** tool: it lives inside every other opener.

Half of our vision is that students *talk their way into mathematics*. Talk moves are the single most transferable skill for making that happen — learn them once and they power every routine you will ever run, and later your Core Instruction discourse too.

blocks.text: The five core talk moves
Based on Chapin, O’Connor & Anderson, *Classroom Discussions in Math*. You don’t need all five at once — start with one.

rows: **Revoicing**
“So you’re saying that… — is that right?”
Clarifies a half-formed idea and gives the student authorship and a chance to correct.
**Restate**
“Who can put what she just said in their own words?”
Makes a second student process the first one’s reasoning; surfaces what was understood.
**Reason**
“Do you agree or disagree, and *why*?”
Pushes students to apply their own reasoning to someone else’s idea.
**Add on**
“Would someone like to add on to that?”
Opens the floor and distributes participation beyond the first responder.
**Wait time**
(silence) “Take your time — I’ll wait.”
5+ seconds of silence dramatically widens who can participate. The hardest move to hold.

blocks.text: Two companions make these work for everyone: **Turn and Talk** (partners rehearse before whole-group) and **Sentence Stems** (posted frames like “I started by…” or “I respectfully disagree because…”).
What it looks and sounds like

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: Students talking *to each other*, not just to the teacher
“I agree with ___ because…” / “Can I add on?”
Comfortable silence (wait time) after a question
The teacher revoicing, then handing it back
A turn-and-talk before big questions
Posted sentence stems students actually use

no.title: We should *not* see
items: Teacher → student → teacher → student ping-pong
“Good job!” ending each idea (evaluation, not discourse)
The same three hands every time
The teacher answering their own question after 1 second
Students competing instead of building together

blocks.text: They are **not** just “more talking,” and they are **not** the teacher praising or correcting each answer. The goal is for the *class* to do the reasoning and evaluating. The moment “good job, that’s right” enters, the thinking stops — students wait for the teacher’s verdict instead of weighing the math themselves.

items: **Turn-and-talk + sentence stems** let multilingual learners rehearse language with a partner before speaking publicly — participation without the spotlight risk.
**Wait time** is an equity move: it shifts who can participate from “the fastest” to “everyone who needs a few seconds to think,” which is most students.
**Revoicing** honors emerging language — a student’s rough idea gets dignified and made usable for the class without being corrected away.
**“Who can add on?”** deliberately distributes status, disrupting the story that only a few students are “good at math.”

blocks.text: Pick **one** move for two weeks — wait time is the highest-leverage place to start. Tell students the new rule out loud (“I’m going to wait, and that’s on purpose”). Add a second move only once the first feels automatic.

blocks.text: Where it lives in the lesson
Talk moves are not a separate activity — they are **how you run every opener**. They sit inside the routine, not beside it.

Whatever opener you choose — a Number Talk, Error Analysis, Quick Images, Same But Different — the talk moves are the mechanism that turns it into a conversation. The same moves carry forward into Core Instruction later, which is why building them now pays off twice.

Your instinct after a student answers is to *respond* (“good, yes, not quite”). The talk-move shift is to *redirect to the class* instead: “What do the rest of you think? Do you agree?” You become the facilitator of the conversation rather than the judge of each answer.
Planning for talk moves (about five minutes)

items: **Pick one or two moves to lean on.** While a routine is new, one is plenty. Wait time first; then “who can add on”; then “do you agree, and why.”
**Plan a turn-and-talk point.** Decide the one moment students will rehearse with a partner before whole-group sharing (usually right after the problem, before answers).
**Post the sentence stems** you want today (see the bank below) so language is supported, not assumed.
**Anticipate one disagreement.** Where might two students see it differently? That is your richest “do you agree, and why?” moment — plan to slow down there.

blocks.text: Mapping the moves to a Number Talk
The moves attach to predictable moments in any routine:

rows: Right after posing the problem
**Wait time** — protect the silence; then a **turn-and-talk**.
Collecting answers
Record all without judgment; **“any other answers?”**
A student shares a strategy
**Revoice** it, then **“who can restate** that in their own words?”
Two strategies are on the board
**“Do you agree or disagree — and why?”** / **“How are these two alike?”**
Participation is narrowing
**“Would someone like to add on?”** + more wait time.
A wrong answer appears
Welcome it: **“What might this person have been thinking?”**

blocks.text: Sentence stem bank (post these for students)
For sharing thinking

items: “I started by…”
“I changed ___ into ___ because…”
“My strategy was to…”
“I knew ___, so…”

blocks.text: For responding to others

items: “I agree with ___ because…”
“I respectfully disagree because…”
“I’d like to add on to…”
“Can you explain why you…?”

blocks.title: Building the norms takes weeks — that’s normal

blocks.text: Students raised on “answer the teacher” won’t discuss on day one. Name the norms explicitly: *talking is how we think here*, *we build on each other*, and *mistakes are useful*. Praise the **behavior you want** (“I love that you built on Maria’s idea”) rather than the correctness of answers.

items: **Always build in the turn-and-talk** — it is the single biggest lever for getting multilingual learners and quieter students into the conversation.
**Keep stems visible all year**, not just at launch; they reduce the language load so students can spend their effort on the mathematics.
**Call on students you primed during turn-and-talk** (“I heard an interesting idea over here…”) so being called on feels safe, not like a gotcha.

blocks.text: Where this leads

The talk moves you build inside openers are exactly what makes **Core Instruction** discourse work — monitoring, selecting, and connecting student strategies all depend on a class that already knows how to reason out loud and build on each other. Master the moves in the low-stakes 10-minute opener, and the harder discourse later lands on prepared ground.
